doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Seminars for students and the business side of music
summary: He advertises seminars on the business of music and describes the cold-calling and symphony Pops work.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Have you had much occasion to visit colleges, and work with college age students?

Not much. I just put an ad in Jazz Times, now available, one of the masters of the jazz cornet Ed Polcer would like to take you on a stroll down Swing Street and perhaps conduct a seminar also if you want involving the business side of music. Things we’re talking about today. I mean I think it could be great for some of the young people. I think it’s a facet that they don’t get. I think if you get clinicians, a lot of musicians are wonderful technicians, I don’t think they can deal with the business side or the history of it, that say I could do. I could present some things for kids to think about. The fact that I spend eight hours a day or six hours a day on the phone and doing paperwork and following up and organizing bands and making those cold calls — hey would you like to book my band? I’m trying to do stuff with the symphony now. I’ve got eight arrangements for jazz band and symphony. We did two symphony concerts last year. A whole new market for new audiences. But try and buck the symphony. They don’t want to do Pops concerts for starters most of the symphonies, they feel it’s a necessary evil. For them it’s like putting on a red vest and playing Dixieland jazz for a picnic, I mean for them playing a Pops concert. So trying to make that sale. But when you talk to kids it’s not just the playing. There’s an awful lot of administrative work that goes into this thing. And you’ve got to be prepared and you’d better have some business courses too. If you’re
going to major in music, take some business courses. But not to be the business of music, but —
Just general knowing business and getting to like people, the whole thing.
